newsitem.title: CHINA: China dissident says no offer of medical parole.
newsitem.headline: China dissident says no offer of medical parole.

text.p: One of China's most prominent dissidents, Wang Dan, told his family during a recent prison visit that Chinese authorities had not offered him medical parole as widely rumoured, his mother said on Tuesday.

"I asked him if the authorities spoke to him about medical parole and he said there has been no such thing," Wang Lingyun said after meeting her son at a prison in the northeastern province of Liaoning last week.
"No one spoke to him about anything," she said in a telephone interview.
Hong Kong newspapers have reported that Chinese authorities had offered to release Wang on condition he leave China.
Wang, 27, was sentenced last year to 11 years in prison for plotting to overthrow the government.
The Chinese-language Wen Wei Po newspaper, mouthpiece of the Chinese Communist Party in Hong Kong, said last month that Wang had agreed to leave for the United States for medical treatment.
Wang's mother declined to speculate on why the pro-Beijing newspaper ran the story.
She said she had not asked Wang if he would be interested in such an opportunity because their meeting in his prison was carried out under tight surveillance.
"He, and we, do not believe there will be this opportunity," she said.
Wang was in poor health, she said, but added that neither the family nor the dissident had requested medical parole.
"His health is not good... (but) he and our family have not up until now requested medical parole," she said. The dissident was suffering from pharyngitis, she said.
Last month, Vice-Minister of Justice Zhang Xiufu said Wang was in good health and did not meet the criteria for medical parole.
A visit to China by U.S. Vice President Al Gore last month fuelled rumours that Beijing would release Wang on medical parole.

Several jailed Chinese dissidents have been released and allowed to leave China to seek medical treatment abroad after they were sentenced following the military crackdown on student-led demonstrations for democracy in June, 1989.
Wang spent four years in jail for his role in the 1989 demonstrations, of which he was a leader, but emerged from imprisonment unbowed.
His case has been repeatedly raised by visiting Western dignitaries, but Beijing dismisses foreign criticism of its human rights record as interference in its internal affairs.

The United States reaffirmed on Monday that it would give full backing to a resolution tabled in the United Nations calling on China to observe human rights and protect the ethnic identity of Tibetans.

The resolution is due to come up for a vote on Tuesday at the U.N. Human Rights Commission in Geneva. China was expected to try to prevent debate on its human rights record by seeking approval of a motion of "no action".

Although U.S. officials privately expressed confidence that they would win good support, diplomats said a Chinese motion for "no action" on the resolution was likely to be passed easily -- as it was last year.
China, mainly with support from Asian and African members of the Commission, has fought off European Union and U.S. efforts to have the U.N. body censure Beijing for the past six years in a row.
